power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < .05", "p < .05", "p > .22", 
"p >= .19"), Text = c("Intensity correlated positively with all three outcomes (rho = .068 to .090, all p < .05).", 
"Breadth and volume, adjusted for session length, were also positively correlated with all three outcomes (breadth: partial rho = .053 to .070; volume: partial rho = .061 to .075; all p < .05).", 
"Framing and reframing and social support practical were used often but were not associated with any outcome (all adjusted p > .22).", 
"Partial Spearman correlations were adjusted for session length (number of worker turns); their unadjusted correlations were small and nonsignificant (rho = .007 to .034, all p >= .19)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .053", "p = .084 ", "p > .22", "p = .053", "p >= .19"), Sentence = c("Social support emotional, the most prevalent technique, was positively associated with understanding before adjustment (b = 0.084, p = .008), but this association fell just short of significance after adjustment (adjusted p = .053).", "Its associations with coping and perspective were weaker (adjusted p = .084 and .198).", "Framing and reframing and social support practical were used often but were not associated with any outcome (all adjusted p > .22).", "Social support (emotional), the most used technique, showed a weaker pattern: its association with understanding fell just short of significance after adjustment (adjusted p = .053), and its associations with coping and perspective were weaker.", "Partial Spearman correlations were adjusted for session length (number of worker turns); their unadjusted correlations were small and nonsignificant (rho = .007 to .034, all p >= .19)." )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

info.title: Toward a Program Theory of A Singaporean Single-Session, Synchronous Chat-Based Mental Health Support for Youths: The Behavior Change Techniques Workers Use and How They Relate to Outcome

								National University of Singapore

									Melbourne
									Australia

text.text: Background: Text-based chat (TBC) services are among the most accessible mental health support for youth, yet more is known about whether they help than about how they help, that is, what workers do in sessions.
Without an account of these worker skills, TBC services cannot be reliably trained for or evaluated.
This study described the techniques chat workers use, drawing on the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy (BCTTv1), and linked them to userreported outcomes.
We analyzed 1,439 real chat sessions (44,916 worker turns) from 73 workers at QuickChat, an anonymous, free, synchronous TBC service for youths aged 12 to 25 in Singapore.
Each worker turn was coded for the presence of 32 behavior change techniques (BCTs).
We examined how often, densely, and broadly techniques were used; how far use varied across workers; and associations with three post-session outcomes: understanding, coping, and perspective.

Results: All 32 techniques appeared, but practice was concentrated in a few: social support (emotional, unspecified, and practical), problem solving, re-attribution, and framing/reframing accounted for three quarters of all instances.
Use varied mainly by session, not by worker, indicating skills shared across the workforce, not individual styles.
Sessions in which workers used more techniques per worker turn received slightly higher ratings on all three outcomes.
Three techniques were each positively associated with all three outcomes: social support (unspecified), problem solving, and pros and cons, though effects were small.
Conclusions: Chat workers deliver change through a small set of core skills, centered on social support and problem solving, and shared across the workforce.
These findings offer a first step toward a program theory of TBC to guide training and evaluation.
Many young people who struggle with mental and emotional issues do not reach professional help.
Stigma, fear of being dismissed, distrust of adults, cost, and limited autonomy in accessing services are well documented barriers to help seeking among youths (Chia et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Stigma, fear of being dismissed, distrust of adults, cost, and limited autonomy in accessing services are well documented barriers to help seeking among youths <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Chia et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Lee et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Text-based chat (TBC) services have grown as a response to these barriers.
These services let young people reach a trained chat worker through synchronous text messaging, usually anonymously, free of charge, and without referral.
They deliver support in a single session rather than a course of treatment (Hoermann et al., 2017).

text.text: Text messaging is a medium young people already use daily, and studies report that chat users find these services acceptable and helpful (Gould et al., 2021).

text.text: Such services now operate in many countries and handle a large volume of youth contacts each year, including the Lifeline Crisis Chat (United States; Gould et al., 2021), Open Up (Hong Kong; Yip et al., 2021), krisenchat (Germany; Eckert et al., 2022), and 113Online (Netherlands; Mokkenstorm et al., 2017), with comparable services in Canada, Denmark, and Finland (Côté & Mishara, 2022; Helfer et al., 2025; Sindahl et al., 2019).

text.text: Outcome evaluation cannot be robust without a clear account of what the intervention involves.

text.text: Building that account from actual practice is missing.
The stakes are practical.
For many young people, TBC is among the most accessible routes into mental health support, reaching those who avoid or cannot access face-to-face care (Gatti et al., 2016; Navarro et al., 2019).

When young adults were asked why they had not used a crisis text service they knew about, the most common answer was that they did not think it would help.

text.text: Seen this way, prior work on this service has mostly captured the mode of delivery, the tone, phrasing, and emoticons that carry a worker's message, and shown that these features predict outcomes.

What those messages do, their change content, the techniques a worker uses to help a chat user cope, reframe, or understand, has not been described with a standard taxonomy, even though it is this content, not its packaging, that a theory of change must specify.
To reconstruct the program theory, we assemble three kinds of evidence.
First, what is delivered and in what dose: which BCTs appear, how often (prevalence and intensity), how much in total (volume), and how many distinct techniques a session draws on (breadth).
Second, whether techniques belong to the service or to individuals.

A BCT used by most workers is plausibly a shared ingredient of the service model, whereas one that varies widely across workers is closer to an individual preference, a distinction that matters for training and quality assurance.
Third, whether techniques are associated with the outcomes chat users report.

Consistent with recommendations that single session chat services be judged on proximal, user reported outcomes rather than symptom scales (Tibbs et al., 2026), we examine three post session outcomes: improved coping, changed perspective, and increased understanding of one's problems.

text.text: Together, these three kinds of evidence, what techniques are used, how consistently, and which track outcomes, produce a first, empirically grounded model of how the service works.
In this study, we analyzed 1,439 real chat sessions from QuickChat, an anonymous, free, synchronous TBC service for youths aged 12 to 25 years in Singapore.
QuickChat does not prescribe a counseling approach for workers to follow, and it does not specify what workers do to bring about change.
To reconstruct one focusing on what workers do in the single session, each worker turn was coded against a shortlist of 32 BCTs from BCTTv1.
We asked three questions.
First, what are the prevalence, intensity, volume, and breadth of BCTs used across sessions?
Second, how much does BCT use vary across chat workers?
Third, are BCTs associated with three chat user reported outcomes at post session: improved coping, changed perspective, and increased understanding?
The findings provide building blocks toward a program theory of TBC.

Knowing what is delivered in a real service, and what appears to work, is a first step toward explaining how this service form brings change, and toward developing TBC into a dependable part of youth mental health care.
The data come from eC2.sg, the digital mental health platform of Fei Yue Community Services in Singapore, which operates QuickChat, an anonymous text-based chatline for youths aged 12 to 25 years.
QuickChat provides free, immediate, synchronous chat: users register with only an email address and are assigned to an available chat worker on duty.

The service operates as a one-session brief intervention and triage platform rather than long term therapy, with the primary objectives of immediate emotional support, situation assessment, and referral (Chung, Lim, et al., 2026; Chung & Lim, 2026).

text.text: Chat workers are clinical professionals (social workers and counsellors) or trained volunteers.
The corpus comprises 1,854 chat sessions from 2016 to 2020.

Within each session, consecutive messages by the same speaker were combined into a single turn, so turns alternate between the chat user and the chat worker; worker turns were the focal unit of coding.

We retained sessions whose chat users completed the post session evaluation questionnaire, giving 44,916 worker turns across 1,439 sessions (mean 31.2 per session), delivered by 73 chat workers (median 8 sessions per worker).
Because service use is anonymous, demographic characteristics of chat users are not available.
Approval for use of the data was obtained from the agency and research ethics approval was obtained from [Blinded for Review] University.
We coded chat workers' use of BCTs using a shortlist of 32 techniques drawn from the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy v1 (BCTTv1; Michie et al., 2013).

text.text: A senior chat worker who supervises the service then selected additional BCTTv1 techniques assessed to be relevant to the type of change work done by chat workers.
Technique definitions followed the BCTTv1 wording.
The full list of the 32 techniques and their definitions is provided in the Supplementary File.
The unit of coding was the worker turn.
Given 44,916 turns and 32 techniques, automated coding was necessary.
Following the approach validated in our previous study (Chung & Lim, 2026), we used a privacy preserving large language model deployed locally (OpenAI's open weight gpt-oss 20b).

text.text: Each worker turn was presented with the chat user turns immediately before and after it as context, with instructions to label the focal turn only.

For every technique, the prompt gave the BCTTv1 definition and a chat context example, and required a presence judgment ("yes", "no", "not sure") made independently for each technique, so a turn could carry multiple techniques.
"Not sure" responses were conservatively recoded as absent.
Full documentation of the labelling pipeline is provided in the Supplementary Material.
To validate the LLM labels, two human coders independently coded a random sample of 200 worker turns against the same technique definitions.
Inter-coder agreement, pooled across the 32 techniques, was almost perfect (Cohen's kappa = 0.90); disagreements were resolved through discussion to produce a gold standard set of labels.
Agreement between the LLM labels and this gold standard was substantial (kappa = 0.80).
From the turn level codes we built session level measures.
For each technique, the primary session metric was its rate per worker turn (count of turns using it divided by the number of worker turns), which accounts for the number of worker turns.
We summarized overall BCT use with three metrics: breadth (distinct BCTs used, range 0 to 32), volume (total BCT events), and intensity (volume divided by length, the number of worker turns).
While breadth and volume both scale with session length, intensity is independent of session length.
At the end of every session, the QuickChat platform directs chat users to a post session evaluation questionnaire.
We used three items, each rated on a 5 point Likert scale (1 = Strongly Disagree to5 = Strongly Agree): • Understanding: "I understand my issues better"
• Coping: "I am able to cope with my issues better"
• Perspective: "I am able to face my issues with a different perspective"
We analyzed the three outcomes separately and did not combine them into a composite.

These items focus on change in the chat user, in how they understand, cope with, and view their problems, consistent with recent work on outcome measurement for helpline services, which distinguishes such help-seeker change from service experience and satisfaction and finds the latter to be prioritised by researchers more than by help-seekers themselves (Curll et al., 2024).

text.text: Analyses followed the three study aims.
All data cleaning and analyses were conducted using R (Version 4.5.3; R Core Team, 2026) and RStudio (Version 2026.4.0.526; Posit team, 2026).
We described each technique's prevalence as the share of worker turns containing it and the share of sessions using it at least once.

We then estimated the correlations between the three session metrics (intensity, volume, and breadth) and the three outcomes using Spearman rank correlations, chosen because the metrics are right skewed and the ratings are bounded with a strong ceiling.
Because session length can inflate volume and breadth, we controlled for session length and computed partial Spearman rank correlations for these two metrics.

This aim asks whether a technique is a shared ingredient of the service model, used at a similar level across the workforce, or reflects a worker's characteristic engagement style, drawn on more by some workers than by others.

The distinction matters for training and quality assurance: a technique that varies mainly from session to session is one the workforce applies in common and can anchor training and fidelity standards, whereas a technique that depends heavily on the worker reflects differences in engagement style across the workforce.
To make this distinction, we computed intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) from null random intercept multilevel models across the 73 chat workers, with sessions nested within workers.
These are "null" models in that they contain no predictors; they only partition the variation in a technique's use into a between worker component and a within worker (session to session) component.

The ICC is the proportion of the total variation that lies between workers: a low ICC means workers use the technique to a similar degree, so its use varies mainly with the session, whereas a high ICC means use depends on the worker, reflecting a difference in engagement style.

We estimated two ICCs per technique, which capture different aspects of use: an intensity ICC, from a linear model of the technique's per turn rate, for how much the technique is used; and an occurrence ICC, from a logistic model of whether the technique was used in the session at all, for whether the worker draws on it at all.
We fitted one linear mixed model per technique per outcome, regressing the 1 to 5 rating on the technique's per turn rate for the session.

As defined for Aim 1, this rate is the count of worker turns using the technique divided by the total number of worker turns in the session, so it expresses how often a worker drew on the technique relative to how much they said, rather than a raw count that would simply grow with session length.
The rate was standardized (z scored across sessions) before entry, so its coefficient reflects a one standard deviation difference in how heavily the technique was used.

We fitted a separate model for each technique rather than entering all techniques together because the aim is descriptive, to characterize each technique's association with outcomes one at a time, and because the techniques are correlated in use, which would make coefficients from a single joint model difficult to interpret.
Session length (the number of worker turns), also standardized, was included as a covariate so that any association reflects how heavily the technique was used rather than how long the session ran.
The random intercept for the chat worker accounts for the nesting of sessions within workers.
Coefficients (b) are the change in the rating, in rating points, per one standard deviation increase in the technique's rate, adjusted for session length and for clustering within worker.
Because we fitted many models (32 techniques by three outcomes), p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure.

Every one of the 32 techniques we coded for appeared in at least one worker turn; none went unused.

text.text: Social support (emotional) appeared in 12.9% of worker turns and in 82.1% of sessions, social support (unspecified) in 6.3% of turns (65.6% of sessions), and social support (practical) in 5.8% of turns (62.7% of sessions).
Together these three social support related techniques made up half of all BCT instances (49.9%).
Problem solving (4.8% of turns), re-attribution (4.3%), and framing and reframing (4.2%) came next.
These six techniques made up three quarters (76.4%) of all BCT instances.
Most techniques saw little use: 25 of the 32 each appeared in fewer than 2% of worker turns.

text.text: At the session level, we summarized technique use with three metrics.
Breadth is the number of distinct techniques a session used at least once.
Volume is the total number of BCT instances in the session.

Intensity is volume divided by the number of worker turns, so it measures how densely techniques were packed into a session; unlike breadth and volume, it does not rise simply because a session is longer.

Sessions drew on several techniques: the average session used 6.1 distinct BCTs (SD = 3.7) with a volume of 15.6 BCT instances (SD = 14.4), giving an intensity of 0.47 BCT instances per worker turn (SD = 0.27).
In other words, techniques appeared at a rate of about one for every two worker turns.

text.text: The technique with most widespread use were social support (emotional; 96% of workers), social support (unspecified; 93%), and problem solving (90%).
The least widespread, mental rehearsal of successful performance, was used by 12% of workers.
This percentage, however, only shows how many workers have ever used a technique.
A worker who used a technique once counts the same as a worker who uses it in every session, so the percentage cannot tell us how far technique use depends on the individual worker.

The ICC (intra-class coefficients) addresses this because ICC is the share of the variation in a technique's use that lies between workers: a high ICC means use depends on who the worker is, while a low ICC means use varies with the session rather than the worker.

text.text: Both ICCs were low.

The median occurrence ICC was 10.6% and the median intensity ICC was 4.0%: for the typical technique, only about 11% of the variation in whether it appeared in a session, and about 4% of the variation in how heavily it was used, could be traced to who the worker was.

The rest of the variation, roughly 89% and 96%, lay between the sessions of the same worker, who would draw on a technique in one session but not the next, and use it more in one and less in another, depending on the session in front of them.

Read together, the occurrence ICC (whether a technique is used at all) and the intensity ICC (how much it is used) point the same way: which techniques are used, and how much, depends far more on the session than on the individual worker.

After each session, chat users rated three items on a 5-point scale from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree): understanding ("I understand my issues better"), coping ("I am able to cope with my issues better"), and perspective ("I am able to face my issues with a different perspective").
Ratings averaged 3.81 (SD = 1.20) for understanding, 3.70 (SD = 1.23) for coping, and 3.72 (SD = 1.23) for perspective.
We then tested whether each technique's rate per worker turn was associated with each of the three ratings, adjusting for session length and accounting for sessions nested within workers.

text.text: Thirteen of the 96 associations were significant, involving six techniques, all positive.
The coefficient b is the change in the outcome rating when a technique's rate per worker turn increases by one standard deviation.

Three techniques were associated with all three outcomes: social support unspecified (b = 0.099 to 0.118, adjusted p = .015 to .027), problem solving (b = 0.096 to 0.114, adjusted p = .015 to .030), and pros and cons (b = 0.089 to 0.102, adjusted p = .025 to .042).
Social support unspecified and problem solving were among the most prevalent techniques, whereas pros and cons was rarely used (0.3% of worker turns, 6.3% of sessions).
Re-attribution was associated with understanding (b = 0.094, adjusted p = .030) and perspective (b = 0.105, adjusted p = .025).
Instruction on how to perform a behavior (b = 0.100, adjusted p = .025) and information about antecedents (b = 0.093, adjusted p = .028) were associated with understanding only.

Social support emotional, the most prevalent technique, was positively associated with understanding before adjustment (b = 0.084, p = .008), but this association fell just short of significance after adjustment (adjusted p = .053).
Its associations with coping and perspective were weaker (adjusted p = .084 and .198).
Framing and reframing and social support practical were used often but were not associated with any outcome (all adjusted p > .22).

These six techniques work on three processes: social support gives the chat user care, encouragement, and practical help, re-attribution and framing and reframing change how the user understands and views their problem, and problem solving helps the user work out what to do next and how to cope (Carey et al., 2018).

text.text: In a chat these are concrete moves: suggesting that a problem may have a different cause than the one the user assumes (re-attribution), offering another way to see the situation (framing and reframing), or working through the options for a next step (problem solving).
The outcome results partly support this account.
Re-attribution was associated with chat users' increased understanding and changes in perspective while problem solving was associated with all three outcomes.

In summary, QuickChat is therefore a service centered on social support, which made up half of all BCT instances, supplemented by techniques that change how users think about their problems and techniques that help them plan.
The combination of BCTs a service uses reflects its underlying theory (Bohlen et al., 2020).

text.text: This profile therefore provides a preliminary account of QuickChat's program theory.

The second finding matters because a program theory describes the service, not Even so, sessions with more instances per turn, more instances in total, and a wider range of techniques had slightly better outcomes, although these associations were small.

One explanation is that each instance gives the session another chance to move one of the processes described above, and a wider range of techniques raises the chance that one of them fits the user's problem.
A program theory for TBC should therefore consider not only which techniques workers use but also how much technique use a session carries.
Future work can test whether training workers to use techniques more often per turn (intensity) and to draw on a wider range of them (breadth) improves outcomes.
The second direction concerns social support and problem solving.
Both were among the most used techniques, and each was associated with all three outcomes.

In a chat, social support (unspecified) is the worker encouraging the user as they work toward coping with the problem, and problem solving is the worker helping the user analyze what stands in the way and choose a way forward.
Together they point to a candidate active ingredient, supportive problem solving: encouraging the user while helping them work out what to do next.
Each technique was tested on its own, however, so whether the two work best in combination remains to be tested.

The problem solving result is consistent with reviews of health behavior interventions, which have linked better outcomes to self-regulatory techniques such as goal setting, from the same BCTTv1 cluster (Dombrowski et al., 2012; Webb et al., 2010).

text.text: The social support result is not, and the setting may explain why.
Those interventions aim to sustain a behavior over weeks or months, such as exercise or diet, whereas a single session chat supports the user through a present problem.
In that setting, the worker's encouragement may itself help the user cope.
Social support may strengthen the user's belief in their ability to cope (Schwarzer & Knoll, 2007) and help them reframe the problem as more manageable (Feeney & Collins, 2015a , 2015b).
text.formatted: Social support may strengthen the user's belief in their ability to cope <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Schwarzer & Knoll, 2007)</ref> and help them reframe the problem as more manageable <ref type="bibr">(Feeney & Collins, 2015a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">, 2015b)</ref>.

text.text: Social support (emotional), the most used technique, showed a weaker pattern: its association with understanding fell just short of significance after adjustment (adjusted p = .053), and its associations with coping and perspective were weaker.
Because it appeared in 82% of sessions, there was little variation in its use from which to detect an association.
It may also act as the base on which a session's change work is built, rather than as a driver of change on its own.
The third direction concerns pros and cons.
In a chat, this is the worker helping the user weigh the reasons for and against a step they are considering, a technique known in motivational interviewing as decisional balance.
It appeared in only 6.3% of sessions and 0.3% of worker turns, yet it was associated with all three outcomes (b = 0.089 to 0.102).
This makes it a candidate for a larger role in the service.
Future work could examine when workers use it, how it combines with problem solving, and why it is used so rarely.

The fourth direction concerns the core techniques that were used often but were not associated with outcomes after adjustment: framing and reframing, social support (practical), and social support (emotional).
This does not mean they have no value.
We tested their rate of use, not how well they were used or how well they fitted the chat user's problem.
These techniques likely depend on that fit: a reframe or a piece of practical help is useful when it matches the user's situation, not when it is frequent.
The open question for these techniques is therefore quality and fit, not amount.
Testing this would mean rating how well each use of a technique matches the problem the chat user describes and how well it is carried out, rather than counting how often it appears.
The effects of the techniques were not tested with a rigorous controlled design.
Techniques were observed as workers used them rather than assigned to sessions, so sessions in which a technique appeared may differ from other sessions in ways we did not measure.
The data also came from one service for youths in Singapore, and worker practices may differ in other services and countries (Higuera-Lozano et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The data also came from one service for youths in Singapore, and worker practices may differ in other services and countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Higuera-Lozano et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The analysis included only sessions whose chat users completed the post session evaluation, and these users may differ from those who did not complete it.
In addition, we measured how often techniques were used, not how well.
Two sessions with the same count of a technique can differ in how skillfully the technique was delivered, and our counts do not capture this difference.
We also examined each technique on its own and did not test how techniques work in combination.

Techniques are typically used in groups rather than alone (Bohlen et al., 2020), and effectiveness often depends on the combination rather than any single technique (Michie et al., 2015), which may be one reason the associations we found were small.
text.formatted: Techniques are typically used in groups rather than alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bohlen et al., 2020)</ref>, and effectiveness often depends on the combination rather than any single technique <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Michie et al., 2015)</ref>, which may be one reason the associations we found were small.

text.text: Our findings begin to open the black box of TBC and give services a program theory to work from (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Our findings begin to open the black box of TBC and give services a program theory to work from (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: In it, change is delivered through a small set of core techniques that every and build fidelity measures to check that the techniques are delivered (Tibbs et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In it, change is delivered through a small set of core techniques that every and build fidelity measures to check that the techniques are delivered <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Tibbs et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A message also has a second layer, its mode of delivery, which is how it is written, including the tone, the phrasing, and features such as emoticons.

The taxonomy keeps these two layers apart. Michie et al. (2013) defined techniques by their mechanism of change rather than their mode of delivery, and removed "tailored personal message" from the taxonomy because it was a mode of delivery, not a technique.
text.formatted: The taxonomy keeps these two layers apart. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Michie et al. (2013)</ref> defined techniques by their mechanism of change rather than their mode of delivery, and removed "tailored personal message" from the taxonomy because it was a mode of delivery, not a technique.

text.text: Both layers matter.
The same technique can be written warmly or flatly, and our earlier work on this service found that the mode of delivery also predicts how chat users rate the session (Chung & Lim, 2026).
text.formatted: The same technique can be written warmly or flatly, and our earlier work on this service found that the mode of delivery also predicts how chat users rate the session <ref type="bibr">(Chung & Lim, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Training and supervision should therefore develop both, the techniques a worker uses and the way the worker writes them.
Finally, we recommend that TBC services treat each session as a single session intervention.

Single session interventions are structured programs that intentionally involve only one encounter with a provider, designed so that a single session can produce meaningful change (Schleider et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Single session interventions are structured programs that intentionally involve only one encounter with a provider, designed so that a single session can produce meaningful change <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Schleider et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings suggest TBC already works in this form.
A single session intervention requires that its one encounter be intentionally structured to do change work, not an unplanned or incidental contact.
Our finding that the core techniques were shared across the workforce, rather than left to individual workers, shows that this change work is deliberate rather than incidental.
Each session therefore carries structured technique use within one contact.

That literature offers concrete resources for practice, including a training stance in which workers treat every session as potentially the last while assuming it can still help, session designs in which the chat user practices a coping skill and leaves with a concrete next step, and outcome expectations matched to what one contact can achieve (Schleider et al., 2023).

text.text: Knowing what produces change within a session is what would make an accessible entry point dependable: a specified account of what the service delivers, which workers can be trained in and evaluators or funders can hold it to.
This study used real transcripts to describe what chat workers do in a TBC service.
The findings speak to the program theory of TBC in two ways.
One set of findings shows what the service delivers now: which techniques workers use, in what amounts, and whether the techniques belong to the service or to individual workers.
The other set shows how the program theory can develop: which techniques, and how much of them, were associated with the outcomes chat users reported, and what still needs testing.
We take each in turn.
The first set of findings shows what QuickChat chat service delivers.
Workers drew on a wide range of techniques, but six formed the core of practice: social support (emotional, individual workers.
If each worker had their own preferred techniques, what QuickChat delivers would depend on who happens to answer the chat, and there would be no single service model to describe.
Our ICCs show the opposite: technique use varied mainly from session to session, not from worker to worker.
The core techniques are therefore shared across the workforce rather than tied to particular workers.
Because they are shared, these techniques can be specified as the service model, taught to every worker, and used as the standard for fidelity checks.
Some worker variation remained, and for the core techniques it lay more in how heavily a technique was used (intensity) than in whether it was used (occurrence).
This was clearest for social support.

For the three social support techniques, the worker accounted for 6.2% to 10.2% of the variation in whether the technique was used in a session (occurrence ICC), but for 8.7% to 19.4% of the variation in how heavily it was used (intensity ICC).
In other words, what the service delivers is largely shared, and what varies by worker is the dose.
A program theory for QuickChat can therefore specify the core skills as part of the service model, while treating how heavily each is used as a point on which workers differ.
The findings so far describe what QuickChat delivers now.
The next question is how the program theory can develop, and the outcome findings point to four directions.
The first direction concerns dosage.
Delivery was at about one BCT instance for every two worker turns.

It was rarely used but was linked to better outcomes.
Workers can consider when it is appropriate, although this finding needs replication.
